title: Pennsylvania couple files lawsuit over Mississippi River cruise collision

 Advertisement Updated: 4:33 PM CST Nov 20, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Metia Carroll Digital editor Pennsylvania couple files lawsuit over Mississippi River cruise collision
 Updated: 4:33 PM CST Nov 20, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Metia Carroll Digital editor NEW ORLEANS — Another lawsuit has been filed in connection with the Mississippi River collision. 
 A Pennsylvania couple who sustained serious injuries from the collision has filed a lawsuit in Orleans Parish Civil District Court, marking the second lawsuit filed in the court. 
 Advertisement Jay and Elizabeth Clymer were vacationing aboard the American Heritage when it was hit by the tanker vessel. 
 Both passengers sustained multiple serious physical injuries during the collision and 
 subsequent rescue efforts.
 Pennsylvania attorney Robert Moran, who associated local New Orleans attorneys Alvendia and Irpino in this matter, said the elderly Clymer couple "barely escaped going into the frigid water only moments before the liner sank into the Mississippi River." 
 Two NOPD first responders sue over Mississippi River crash: 
 Two New Orleans police officers who say they were injured while helping rescue people after a tanker struck a docked cruise ship have filed a lawsuit against the tanker’s owner and manager.
 Cedric Davillier and Regina Williams filed the lawsuit Nov. 18 in Orleans Parish Civil District Court. The complaint identifies them as NOPD first responders who went to the scene of the Nov. 13 collision between the tanker Atlantic Asphalt and the American Heritage at the Thalia Street Terminal. 
 The lawsuit names Nave Shipping SA, which it identifies as the tanker's owner, and Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd., which it says managed or operated the vessel.
 The plaintiffs allege the tanker was unseaworthy, its crew was improperly trained, and the defendants failed to account for conditions on the Mississippi River or take steps to avoid the collision. They say they suffered significant injuries to their minds and bodies while trying to rescue passengers and crew.
 They seek damages for physical and emotional pain, medical expenses, lost wages, loss of earning capacity and loss of enjoyment of life. The complaint also seeks punitive damages under maritime law.
 The allegations have not been proven in court. The plaintiffs requested a jury trial.
 Port of New Orleans files lawsuit
 The Port of New Orleans also filed a federal lawsuit and obtained an arrest warrant for the tanker after it collided with the river cruise ship on Friday.
 Court records show the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans filed the lawsuit against Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping and Thome Ship Management.
 The federal docket lists a $1 million demand in the maritime property damage case.
 Court records also show the port requested a warrant to arrest the tanker, which a federal judge granted. The warrant was then issued.
 Experts explained that a ship arrest is a temporary measure designed to freeze a vessel in port, providing financial security for an unpaid creditor or claimant.
 Claimants can request an arrest for issues such as unpaid crew wages, cargo damage or collision damage.
 The ship remains detained until the owner posts adequate financial security, such as a bank guarantee or cash deposit.
 "Typically, what happens is once the vessel is seized, the owner comes to court, posts a bond in lieu of the vessel. Then the vessel can go on its way, while the bond will stand as essentially the rest that could be used to satisfy any judgments against the vessel," experts said.
 Lawyers said this is the early stage of the lawsuit, which could take years to settle.
 Ongoing Vessel Recovery and Investigation 
 The Unified Command, consisting of the U.S. Coast Guard and American Cruise Lines, continues to coordinate technical shoreside and waterborne surveys to inform salvage operations. The Unified Command’s priorities remain ensuring the safety of response personnel and the public, protecting the marine environment, and facilitating the safe and efficient salvage of the vessel.
 Lightering operations aboard the American Heritage began Tuesday, with crews beginning the removal of fuel from the vessel.
 The Unified Command continues to monitor for signs of pollution and assess potential environmental impacts. The safety of response personnel and the public, protection of the marine environment, and safe salvage of the vessel remain the Unified Command's top priorities.
 River traffic:
 A safety zone remains in effect on the Mississippi River between mile markers 95.5 and 96.5, extending 500 feet from the east bank.
 The alternate channel within this area remains closed to maritime traffic.
 Limited two-way vessel traffic is permitted through the main span; however, deep-draft vessels and towing vessels with 10 or more barges are restricted to one-way transit.
 Investigation continues:
 The NTSB continues to lead the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the collision.
 The NTSB is asking anyone with photographs or video footage of the incident to submit them directly to witness@ntsb.gov .
